title: Living ashtpadi 23
hookLine: clear sight is a gift, not a skill

lines: THE FIRST WEEK: YOU NOTICE EVERYTHING.
cards: The first week in a new apartment, you notice everything: the way the light hits the kitchen at four o'clock, the creak in the third stair, the neighbor's wind chime.
A year later, you walk past all of it without a glance. Nothing changed. The light still comes in at four.
You just stopped seeing it. That fading is ordinary, and easy to miss. The twenty-third ashtpadi has something to say about it, from an unexpected direction.

teach.b: Here's the twenty-third ashtpadi in brief. The Guru applies giaan anjan, the eye-ointment of wisdom, and the darkness of not-knowing ends.
With cleared eyes, God is seen within and without, at both ends of every look, the seer and the seen. The natural modern response: great, how do I train my eyes? What's the technique?
Sukhmani gently sets that aside. Look again at the salok. Who gave the ointment?
The Guru. How did the seeker meet the holy one?

teach.h: HAR KIRPAA TE: BY GOD'S GRACE.
teach.b: Har kirpaa te: by God's grace. Clear sight, in this ashtpadi, isn't a skill you master like a language or a golf swing. It's a gift you receive.
That doesn't make practice pointless. Sikh practice still includes amrit vela, the company of the sangat, recitation.
One way to picture it: practice is more like opening the shutters than building a lamp. In the salok's picture, the light comes from elsewhere. You can make room for it; you can't manufacture it.
And there's real freedom in that.

teach.h: A BLURRY DAY IS NOT A FAILURE.
teach.b: If seeing freshly were a skill, every dull, blurry day would be your failure.
If it's a gift, a blurry day is just a day the shutters stuck, and tomorrow the light may come in again. The salok's last word is pargaas, the mind lit up.
Not lit by effort; lit, the way a room is when the sun comes through.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that clear sight comes by God's grace and the Guru's wisdom, and they keep daily practice as a way of making room for that light.

o: the flame of a lamp lit at prayer
light, the mind lit up from within
a burst of insight you earn by study

p: the shutters stuck, not a failure

s: in Sukhmani, clear sight is a technique you master
the salok says it comes by God's grace and the Guru's gift.
Sikhs still keep daily practice, even though sight is a gift
practice makes room for the light, like opening shutters.
the salok ends with the word pargaas, light
the mind lit up, the way a room is lit by the sun.

games.q: it's a dull day, and nothing looks fresh. by the twenty-third ashtpadi, what is this?
o: a day the shutters stuck; the light may come tomorrow.
a sign to give up practice.
games.why: clear sight is a gift, not a skill, so a blurry day isn't your failure. you keep the shutters open, and the light comes by grace.

practice: Choose something you see every day and never notice, a doorframe, a mug, the view from your usual chair, and look at it as if you'd just moved in: its color, its shape, a scratch, the way light lands on it.
Don't force a feeling; leave the shutters open, and if nothing comes in, that's fine too. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look.

wordCard.voice: Pargaas, light or illumination: clear sight comes by grace, har kirpaa te; practice opens the shutters, and pargaas comes in.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pargaas, light or illumination; the salok's last word, the mind lit up.

carryVoice: Your line: see freshly. Shutters open; the light that comes in is grace. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 23 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 293–294)
